title: Perfect sampling of Ising spin glasses with bounding chains
abstract: We study perfect sampling algorithms for Ising spin glasses based on coupling from the past and bounding chains, on several graph families and coupling distributions. For the single-site bounding chain, we establish coalescence in $O(n\log n)$ updates under Dobrushin conditions. On sparse random graphs, our numerical results suggest that efficient sampling extends throughout the tree-uniqueness regime, with a slowdown beyond this threshold. On Erdős-Rényi random graphs $\mathcal{G}(n,d/n)$ with standard Gaussian couplings, we introduce a block bounding chain and prove its coalescence in $O(n\log n)$ block updates in the tree-uniqueness regime for sufficiently large $d$, each block update requiring $O(n)$ operations, adapting a proof in~\cite{Efthymiou_Zampetakis_2024} for the rapid mixing of block Glauber dynamics. On periodic lattices, our experiments instead suggest that the single-site bounding chain is limited by the looseness of its bounding envelope, whereas on the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model, slow coalescence is accompanied by damage spreading at every inverse temperature tested. These observations motivate alternative bounding representations and couplings as strategies to improve perfect sampling on spin glasses.
summary: This work analyzes perfect sampling algorithms for Ising spin glasses using bounding chains, establishing theoretical bounds on coalescence time for certain random graph structures. The authors compare these results across different graph types, demonstrating that algorithmic efficiency is limited by factors like the tightness of the bounding envelope or the onset of damage spreading. This provides critical insights into the computational feasibility of simulating complex disordered quantum systems.
main_problem: The paper investigates the efficiency and theoretical limits of perfect sampling algorithms, specifically using bounding chains, for Ising spin glasses.
main_result: The authors prove rapid coalescence of the bounding chain in the tree-uniqueness regime for Gaussian couplings on random graphs, while observing limitations due to the bounding envelope or damage spreading on lattices and the SK model.
method: The study combines theoretical proofs, adapting coupling estimates from block dynamics, with extensive numerical simulations across various graph families.
model_or_system: The system is the Ising spin glass defined on a graph G=(V, E) with a Gibbs measure governed by couplings J. The analysis covers sparse random graphs, periodic lattices, and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model.
key_observables: Coalescence time ($T_{	ext{coal}}$) of the bounding chain, damage spreading, and the tree-uniqueness regime.
important_parameters: Inverse temperature ($ eta$), graph connectivity ($d$), and the system size ($n$).
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on the Dobrushin condition or the assumption of the tree-uniqueness regime for establishing rapid mixing/coalescence.
figures_summary: Figures show empirical scaling of the rescaled coalescence time ($T_{	ext{coal}}/n$) for various graph models (random $d$-regular, lattices, SK) and the evolution of the mean number of unresolved sites ($E[W_t]$) over time.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the sampling problem, developing the bounding chain framework, proving coalescence for specific random graph models, and then empirically testing and analyzing the limitations of this method on lattices and the SK model.
why_interesting: While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the techniques for analyzing convergence rates and identifying algorithmic thresholds in complex energy landscapes (like spin glasses) are highly relevant to understanding dynamics in quantum many-body systems and quantum simulation algorithms.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: Fraction of coalesced runs on G(n, d/n) with d = 4, i.i.d. uniform couplings in {+1, −1} (left panel) and i.i.d. standard Gaussian couplings (right panel). We set Thor = 109 single-site updates, and nruns = 50. The corresponding tree-uniqueness threshold is βuni ≃0.2554 (left) and βuni ≃0.3349 (right).

Figure 2: Empirical mean of the rescaled coalescence time Tcoal/n as a function of n on logarithmic axes, for G(n, d/n) with d = 4. Couplings are i.i.d., drawn uniformly from {+1, −1} (left) or from the standard Gaussian distribution (right).

Figure 3: Rescaled empirical mean coalescence time as a function of n, on random 4-regular graphs (top panels) and on periodic 2-dimensional lattices (bottom panels). Couplings are i.i.d. drawn from {+1, −1}. The curves show the corresponding rescalings of two fits: Tcoal = an log n + bn (dashed line) and Tcoal = cnδ (dotted line)

Figure 4: Evolution of the mean number of unresolved sites E[Wt] on random d-regular graphs with d = 4, i.i.d. couplings uniform in {+1, −1}, averaged over 50 independent runs. Left panel: E[Wt] as a function of the number of single-site updates, for n = 105

Figure 5: Number of unresolved (star) sites against iterations, averaged over nruns = 50 runs, for β values below and above βuni on small system sizes (n = 100), on G(n, 4/n) (left panel, βuni ≃0.255413) and on random 4-regular graphs (right panel, βuni ≃0.346574) with i.i.d. couplings uniform in {+1, −1}.
